title: Graded degradation profiles and failover playbook for downstream deps (Redis/Kafka/DB)
creator: Riley Park
description: Summary: Define and implement a graded degradation model, region-aware failover playbook, and connection-pool/circuit-breaker rules for critical downstream systems (Redis, Kafka, primary DB) to keep Redwood's inference API within SLOs during partial dependency outages or degradation. Goals: reduce user-visible errors, limit cost/regret during incidents, provide deterministic fallbacks per request class, and make behavior observable and testable.
detailed_plan:
1) Degradation profiles (per-dependency)
- Level 0 (Normal): Full feature set, normal timeouts and pool sizes.
- Level 1 (Conservative): Lower concurrency for non-critical paths, longer KV cache TTL, prefer local stale cache (stale-while-revalidate up to 30s), sampling for telemetry to reduce load.
- Level 2 (Economy): Redirect writes to buffered spool (disk-backed) for non-blocking ingestion; reads use read-replica or last-good-value; enable aggressive prefix/KV cache hit reuse; drop low-priority background work.
- Level 3 (Read-only / Best-effort): Disable non-essential writes, enable 503 with Retry-After for tenant-level heavy operations, continue critical reads only with bounded staleness.
- Level 4 (Circuit-open): Serve cached or synthetic responses for a subset of routes, return deterministic errors for strongly-consistent operations.

Mapping to dependencies:
- Redis (session/cache): Try local in-memory LRU fallback -> stale-while-revalidate -> cached TTL extension -> read-only fallback -> error. Use “approx-consistent” path for conversational KV (store locally then async write-back).
- Kafka (event ingestion / streaming): For producers: buffer to disk spool + backpressure in-flight hedging -> drop non-critical telemetry with probabilistic sampling -> switch to direct S3 archival for backlog. For consumers: switch to reduced partition consumers with prioritized consumer groups.
- Primary DB (writes/reads): Prefer read-replicas for read-heavy endpoints with explicit staleness budget. For writes: if primary rejects, buffer writes for short windows or return a clear user-facing error for strongly-consistent mutations.

2) Circuit breaker design
- Two-tier breakers: soft (adaptive throttling) and hard (open/close) per dependency + per-tenant where applicable.
- Soft threshold: triggered when p95 latency > SLO*1.75 for 3 consecutive 60s windows -> reduce concurrency weight for that dependency by 30% and enable aggressive caching.
- Hard threshold: error rate > 5% sustained over 2 minutes or connection failure > 50% over 1 minute -> open for initial 20s, then half-open probe with 5% traffic.
- Metrics used: p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, connection saturation, queue depth, CPU/GPU pressure on serving nodes.

3) Connection pooling & allocation
- Dynamic per-dependency pool sizing based on request-class weights (priority queueing). Attach a per-request “priority score” derived from route, tenant, and model-criticality.
- Soft quota buckets per pool: normal, reserved (high-priority), and opportunistic. Opportunistic requests get evicted first.
- Pool eviction policy: LRU + request-priority bias. When pool saturates, shed opportunistic work and route critical flows to alternate region/replica.

4) Load-shedding and admission control
- Request scoring: cheap deterministic score combining tenant SLA, route importance, and model latency sensitivity.
- Admission policy: token-bucket per-region + global concurrency semaphore. When tokens exhausted, drop opportunistic and return guidance with Retry-After + telemetry id for debugging.
- Progressive shedding: prefer to shed background/analysis and sampling traffic before user-facing inference calls.

5) Multi-region failover
- Region-aware routing: prefer local region; on degraded P95 > threshold for 30s, route new requests to next-best region (with warm caches and cold-start mitigation). Add routing policy to prefer model variant that is cheaper/lower memory if needed.
- KV/DB replication: ensure read-after-write consistency guarantees are surfaced to API clients when we promote a different region; offer explicit eventual-consistency flag for clients that can accept it.

6) Observability & SLOs
- Per-route SLOs: latency p95 and availability (4xx/5xx) per tenant tier, per model variant.
- Dashboards: dependency health (latency, errors), pool saturation, circuit-breaker state, shed rate by route, per-tenant impact heatmap.
- Alerts: multi-stage (warning at 10% SLO burn rate over 15m, page at 50% burn over 5m). Include synthetic probes that exercise fallback paths.

7) Testing & rollout
- Canary plan: internal canary -> staged canary on low-traffic tenants -> broader rollout with feature flag.
- Chaos tests: simulate high latency on Redis/Kafka/DB in staging, validate routing, buffering, and client-visible behavior.
- Regression tests: integration tests for buffer durability, spool replay, half-open behavior.

8) Runbook & playbook
- Document step-by-step actions for: identify the dependency causing SLO breach, determine degradation level, trigger automated actions (scale, change routing), and manual remediation steps.
- Include templates for customer communication for P1 incidents.
acceptance_criteria:
- Automated degradation profiles can be toggled by feature flag and produce expected behavior in staging chaos runs.
- Circuit-breaker transitions observable in dashboards with correct metrics emitted (state_change events).
- Measured p95 for critical routes stays within SLO or shows documented graceful degradation with clear customer messaging.
- End-to-end tests for buffered writes and spool replay pass in CI.
risks_and_tradeoffs:
- Buffering writes increases operational complexity (durability and replay correctness). We must cap spool size and provide backpressure to avoid OOMs.
- Aggressive caching/staleness exposes users to stale data; must be limited to non-critical flows and surfaced in API docs.
- Multi-region routing raises cross-region egress costs and potential consistency surprises for clients; require opt-in for eventual consistency in some APIs.
